lines.caption: This is a tour of pull request 36, which makes the desktop and the laptop install each new CI build by themselves.
lines.say: This is a tour of pull request thirty-six, which makes the desktop and the laptop install each new C I build by themselves.

lines.caption: It has three parts: what this PR adds, how it was built and verified, and the rollout on both machines.
Part 1. What this PR adds.
A timer runs the updater two minutes after boot, then every hour, and catches up after sleep.
The updater asks GitHub for the latest release, with a read-only token only root can read.
It reads the version from inside the downloaded package and compares it with the installed one.
If they differ, it installs all three packages together, even when that means going back a version.
Then, if Thunar is running, a notification asks you to restart it. Failures notify you too.
Thunar is never restarted for you; the new build loads when you restart it.
Since issue 1, every merge publishes the packages as a GitHub release; now each machine installs them by itself.
Because it installs whatever is latest, deleting a bad release rolls both machines back within the hour.
When the version hasn't changed, it remembers that release, so later checks download nothing.
An apt pin keeps this build installed and blocks Zorin's Thunar packages from replacing it.
lines.say: An apt pin keeps this build installed and blocks Zorin's Thunar packages from replacing it.

lines.caption: A one-time setup script installs everything, asks for the token without showing it, and starts the timer.
All of it lives in a new deploy folder, plus this page and its narration.
To go back to Zorin's Thunar, turn off the timer, install the saved Zorin packages, and delete the pin.
Part 2. How it was built and verified.
The updater ran against a fake GitHub in the cloud container, serving stand-in packages.
It installed, upgraded, and rolled back, and sent one notification for each install.
A bad token failed three runs in a row but notified once; an unreachable GitHub was retried quietly.
With the pin in place, a newer Zorin version was refused, and nothing was upgraded.
The setup script ran with the system commands stubbed out, and installed the files with the right permissions.
Real GitHub and the real machines were not tested here; that happens in the rollout.
A fresh review agent found three problems, and all three are fixed.
The worst: the repo ignores service files, so the service unit was missing from the commit.
Token errors now name the token, and a repeating failure notifies once instead of every hour.
Downloading with your token, the upgrade on the desktop, and updates after a merge come only after the merge.
Part 3. What comes later: the rollout on both machines.
First, create a read-only token for this repo on GitHub.
Then run the setup on the desktop, update once, and check the notification appears.
Then run the same setup on the laptop.
Finally, merge a small change, and both machines should update within the hour.
After the desktop updates, restart Thunar and run the split-view crash check once.
From now on, each merge reaches both machines on its own, and you choose when to restart Thunar.
